# Central bank and lender of last resort (`central_bank`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/economy.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Economy & finance (`economy`)
- Deps: needs banking_credit; helped by paper_money, public_debt_bonds, quantity_theory_inflation
- Core idea: One bank holds the government's account and the reserves of the other banks and usually has the monopoly of issuing notes. It keeps the money's value steady by changing the rate at which it lends (the discount rate) and by buying or selling securities. In a panic it is the lender of last resort: following Bagehot's rule it lends freely to sound banks against good security at a high rate, so that depositors see they can be paid and the run stops, while insolvent banks are allowed to fail. It must be shielded from the treasury, or it becomes a printing press for deficits.
- Pitfalls:
  - Letting it finance the government's deficits: Law's Banque Royale (1720) and the Reichsbank (1923)
  - Standing aside in a panic: sound banks fail with the unsound (United States 1930–1933)
  - Rescuing every bank and its owners: they then take ever bigger risks (moral hazard)
  - Thinking the early banks were founded as central banks: the Bank of England was set up in 1694 to lend to the king and learned the role over 150 years
- History: europe: 1609 – Amsterdam Wisselbank, a public exchange bank with stable bank money; 1668 Sveriges Riksbank, the oldest still existing; 1694 Bank of England; 1800 Banque de France; 1844 Bank Charter Act; 1866 Overend Gurney crisis and 1873 Bagehot's Lombard Street; 1876 Reichsbank; islamic: 1863 – Imperial Ottoman Bank acts as state bank and note issuer; east_asia: 1882 – Bank of Japan; americas: 1913 – Federal Reserve; india: 1935 – Reserve Bank of India; china: 1928 – Central Bank of China (Nationalist government)
- Read:
  - Walter Bagehot, Lombard Street: A Description of the Money Market (1873)
  - Charles Goodhart, The Evolution of Central Banks (1988)
  - Charles P. Kindleberger, Manias, Panics, and Crashes (1978)
